analysis.one_liner: Creates a public health insurance option, expands premium subsidies, and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor from either party, and died in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a government-run health insurance plan sold alongside private plans on the ACA marketplaces, paying doctors and hospitals Medicare rates. It would have raised the income cap for premium subsidies from 400% to 600% of the federal poverty level, required drug manufacturers to pay rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, and let the government negotiate prescription drug prices and offer its own nationwide Medicare drug plan at a $37 monthly premium. It was introduced on the first day of the 116th Congress and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying insurance on the ACA marketplaces would gain a lower-cost public plan competing with private insurers, and middle-income households between 400% and 600% of poverty would become newly eligible for premium subsidies. Low-income Medicare enrollees would benefit from mandatory drug rebates, and all Medicare beneficiaries would gain a government-negotiated, nationwide drug plan option at a $37 monthly premium.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace buyers, middle-income families, Medicare enrollees

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public health insurance option on the ACA exchanges that pays providers at Medicare rates, giving consumers a lower-cost alternative to private plans; Medicare-level payment rates are generally well below what private insurers pay.

Raises the income ceiling for ACA premium tax credits from 400% to 600% of the federal poverty level, extending help to middle-income families who currently get none, and limits repayment of excess advance credits.

Requires drug manufacturers, as a condition of participating in Medicare Part D, to pay rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees at least as large as their Medicaid rebates; manufacturers that refuse lose Part D coverage for their drugs.

Deletes the Part D 'noninterference' provision so the government can negotiate drug prices like other bulk purchasers, and creates a nationwide government-run prescription drug plan with a $37 monthly premium in 2021, guaranteeing every Medicare beneficiary a public plan option plus at least two private choices.
Fully reimburses qualified retiree prescription drug plans and equalizes their subsidies so retirees in those plans are not penalized.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would pay new mandatory rebates and face government price negotiation, with refusal costing them Part D coverage. Private insurers would face a government-run competitor on the exchanges and in the Part D market. Doctors and hospitals would be paid at Medicare rates rather than higher private rates by the public option. Taxpayers would front $2 billion in start-up funding plus 90 days of claims reserves, which the plan must repay over ten years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers, private insurers, providers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The plan requires a $2 billion federal start-up appropriation plus 90 days of claims reserves, and its premiums must fully finance its own costs, so the government is on the hook if enrollment projections fall short.

Paying providers at Medicare rates, roughly what the government already pays seniors, means hospitals and physicians would take in less from public-option patients than from private insurance, which providers argued could pressure rural and safety-net hospitals.

Even the negotiation provision is hedged: the bill forbids the Secretary from requiring a national formulary or imposing a price structure, so the government negotiates without the main lever other countries use, and there is no judicial review of payment rates.
The public option is available only through the exchanges, so its reach is limited to the individual market and would not directly affect the employer coverage most working people have.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for consumers are real and broad: cheaper public coverage on the exchanges, subsidies reaching further up the income scale, and downward pressure on drug prices through rebates and negotiation. The main costs fall on drug manufacturers and private insurers, with a temporary $2 billion federal outlay that the plan must repay. The honest caveats are that providers would absorb Medicare-level payments, and the negotiation authority is written without a national formulary, making it weaker than negotiation systems abroad. On balance the bill was a moderate, market-based version of health reform rather than a sweeping one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never held a hearing or a vote, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cardin introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over Medicare, tax credits, and prescription drug policy.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor, and the Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the entire two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and private health insurers are better off, because the rebates, price negotiation, and public-plan competition never advanced. Providers also kept higher private payment rates. Consumers who might have bought into a public option or qualified for newly expanded subsidies gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Benjamin Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee; it was his opening-day proposal for the 116th Congress.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat without action from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors — from Republicans and from Cardin's own Democrats — and never came to a vote, so support never split along party lines in any measurable way.

industries.note: The bill imposes Medicaid-style rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, authorizes government price negotiation, and strips Part D coverage from manufacturers that refuse. Drug makers charge Medicare far more than negotiated systems abroad, so the bill's savings come directly out of their revenue.

A government-run plan paying Medicare rates would compete with private plans on the exchanges, and a $37-a-month public drug plan would compete in Part D. Insurers profit from the absence of a public benchmark, so the bill's benefit to consumers is their cost.

The public option pays providers at Medicare rates, which are well below private commercial rates, cutting revenue per patient. Expanded subsidies and more affordable coverage would modestly increase the number of insured patients, partially offsetting the lower rates.
